75 per cent of the revenue goes to the cantons, 25 per cent to the Confederation.
In the OECD project, the minimum tax is called “Pillar Two”.
In June 2025 the G7 agreed on exceptions for US corporations.

abschnitte.text: Many countries try to attract companies with **low taxes on profits**. This is called **tax competition**. The minimum tax is meant to put a floor under this competition. Countries should no longer undercut each other with ever lower taxes. Large corporations should bear a **minimum tax burden** everywhere, no matter where they declare their profits.

The minimum tax rate is **15 per cent**. It applies only to large groups of companies with an annual turnover of at least **750 million euros**. The vast majority of small and medium-sized businesses in Switzerland are not affected. If a corporation's tax in a country is below 15 per cent, a **top-up tax** can be charged.

The minimum tax came out of the OECD/G20 project **BEPS**. This stands for “Base Erosion and Profit Shifting”. It is aimed at tax tricks with which corporations shift profits to **low-tax countries**. The project has two pillars. **Pillar One** redistributes taxing rights to the countries where goods are sold. **Pillar Two** governs the minimum tax.

abschnitte.titel: Putting it into effect in Switzerland
abschnitte.text: To put it into effect, the **Federal Constitution** had to be changed. On **18 June 2023**, about **79 per cent** of voters approved the proposal. The top-up tax has applied since **1 January 2024**. **75 per cent** of the revenue goes **to the cantons** and **25 per cent to the Confederation**. The cantons get three quarters because they are responsible for company taxes and compete with each other on taxes.

The **USA** has its own rules for a minimum tax and rejected parts of the OECD solution. In June 2025 the **G7** agreed on a “side-by-side” approach. Under it, US corporations are exempted from parts of the global minimum tax. In return, the USA dropped planned retaliatory taxes. What happens next is still being negotiated internationally.

gewusst: In 2021 more than 130 countries agreed to the principle of a global minimum tax.
It is mainly cantons with many international corporations, such as Zug or Basel-Stadt, that receive revenue from the top-up tax.

teile.einleitung: Free trade means that goods are traded between countries with no customs duties or only a few. Switzerland is a small country with many exports and so depends heavily on open trade. At the same time it protects some areas, above all farming.
wichtigste: Customs duties are charges on imported goods and are often meant to protect home-grown products.
Since 1 January 2024 Switzerland has no longer charged customs duties on industrial products.
There are still customs duties on many farm products such as meat.
The World Trade Organization WTO has its seat in Geneva and was founded in 1995.
Switzerland is a founding member of EFTA.
Since 1972 a free trade agreement with the EU has applied to industrial goods.

abschnitte.text: A **customs duty** is a charge you have to pay when you bring goods into a country. Customs duties make foreign goods **more expensive**. This way **home producers** have less competition. The state also takes in money. **Free trade** means the opposite: customs duties and other barriers to trade are removed, so that goods can cross borders more easily.

Since **1 January 2024** Switzerland has **no longer charged customs duties** on **industrial products** such as bicycles, clothes or cars. This is meant to make goods cheaper for companies and consumers. It is different for **farming**: on many **agricultural products**, for example **meat** or dairy products, there are still customs duties, some of them high. In this way Switzerland wants to protect its **farms**.

The **World Trade Organization WTO** sets rules for world trade. It has its seat in **Geneva**. The WTO was founded in **1995** and replaced the **GATT**, an agreement on tariffs and trade from **1947**. When countries argue about trade, the WTO can help to **settle the dispute**. Most countries in the world are members.

The **European Free Trade Association EFTA** was founded in **1960**. Switzerland is a **founding member**. Today its members are Switzerland, **Norway**, **Iceland** and **Liechtenstein**. Through EFTA, Switzerland concludes many **free trade agreements** with other countries. In **1972** it concluded a **free trade agreement** for industrial goods with what was then the European Economic Community. The people approved it clearly in December 1972.

Supporters say that free trade makes goods cheaper and creates jobs in exporting companies. Critics fear that home businesses come under pressure or that environmental standards suffer. How important open markets are became clear in **2025**: from **7 August 2025** the **USA** charged a customs duty of **39 per cent** on many Swiss goods, for example machines and watches. After negotiations the rate was lowered to **15 per cent** in November 2025.

gewusst: Switzerland earns a large part of its prosperity from exports, for example of medicines, machines and watches.
The 1972 agreement with today's EU still applies today.

teile.einleitung: An aid organisation is an organisation that helps people in need. Aid organisations collect donations and use the money for projects. In Switzerland there are many well-known aid organisations that work at home and abroad.
wichtigste: Aid organisations help people in need, in Switzerland and abroad.
Pro Juventute runs the number 147 for children and young people.
Terre des hommes was founded in Lausanne in 1960.
The Pestalozzi Children's Village has stood in Trogen since 1946.
Caritas belongs to the Catholic Church, HEKS to the Reformed Church.
The ZEWO seal of approval shows that an aid organisation handles donations carefully.

abschnitte.text: Aid organisations collect **money** and use it to help people in need. Some help after disasters; others support children, families or mountain farmers. Many work with **donations** from private people. Often **volunteers**, who are not paid, also help. Most aid organisations are organised as an association or a foundation.

**Pro Juventute** works for children and young people in Switzerland. On the number **147** they can get advice and help round the clock. **Terre des hommes** was founded in Lausanne in 1960 by Edmond Kaiser and helps children in need. The **Pestalozzi Children's Village** was founded in 1946 in Trogen in the canton of Appenzell Ausserrhoden. At first, children who had lost their parents in the war lived there.

Some aid organisations belong to churches. **Caritas** is the aid organisation of the Catholic Church. It helps poor people in Switzerland and abroad. **HEKS** is the aid organisation of the Protestant Reformed Church of Switzerland. HEKS also works at home and abroad. Both help everyone, regardless of their religion.

**Swiss Mountain Aid** supports farming families and businesses in the mountains. This way people can go on living and working there. The **Swiss Red Cross**, for example, helps older people or trains babysitters. **Swiss Solidarity** (the Glückskette) collects money after disasters and passes it on to Swiss aid organisations.

The **ZEWO** foundation checks aid organisations. Those that carry its **seal of approval** use donations honestly and carefully. Children can also help, for example with a **sponsored run**. Adults pay an amount for every lap run. The money then goes to an aid project.

gewusst: Pro Juventute's number 147 can also be reached by chat and text message.
Today children from different countries meet at the Pestalozzi Children's Village in Trogen for exchange projects.

teile.einleitung: The Group of Seven, G7 for short, is a meeting of seven large industrialised countries with democratic governments. Their heads of state and government meet every year for a summit. There they talk about the economy, security and global problems.
wichtigste: The G7 is made up of the USA, Japan, Germany, France, Great Britain, Italy and Canada.
The European Union also takes part in the meetings.
The first summit took place in 1975 at the Château de Rambouillet near Paris.
The G7 is an informal forum with no founding treaty and no permanent secretariat.
Russia was part of it for a time but was excluded in 2014 after the annexation of Crimea.
The 2026 summit took place in Évian on Lake Geneva.

abschnitte.text: In 1975 the French President **Valéry Giscard d'Estaing** and the German Chancellor **Helmut Schmidt** invited leaders to a meeting. It took place at the **Château de Rambouillet** near Paris, with six countries at the time. The background was the **oil crisis** and the end of the Bretton Woods system of fixed exchange rates. A year later Canada joined, and so the G7 was created.

abschnitte.titel: From G7 to G8 and back
abschnitte.text: In the 1990s **Russia** was admitted to the group, which was then called the **G8**. After the annexation of the Ukrainian peninsula of **Crimea** in 2014, the other members suspended Russia's participation. Since then the group has met as the G7 again. Besides the G7, since 1999 there has been the **G20**, which also includes large emerging economies such as China, India and Brazil.

The G7 is not an international organisation like the WTO or the UN. It has **no founding treaty** and no permanent secretariat. The **presidency** changes every year, and the country holding it organises the summit. The meetings are prepared by the leaders' personal representatives, the so-called **sherpas**. Decisions are political statements of intent, not laws.

In 2025 Canada held the presidency and invited leaders to **Kananaskis** in the Rocky Mountains. In 2026 it was France's turn. The summit took place from 15 to 17 June in **Évian-les-Bains** on Lake Geneva. Many delegations arrived via **Geneva Airport**, where the President of the Confederation, Guy Parmelin, welcomed them. The Swiss Army helped with security. But Switzerland is not a member of the G7.

gewusst: Évian had already hosted a summit in 2003, at that time of the G8.
The name “sherpa” for the people who prepare summits comes from the mountain guides in the Himalayas, who clear the way to the summit for others.

teile.einleitung: Global governance means countries and organisations managing worldwide problems together. Problems such as climate change, pandemics or financial crises do not stop at national borders. That is why many countries, international organisations and also companies and aid organisations have to work together.
wichtigste: Global governance means something like governing or steering the world together.
There is no world government, so cooperation is needed.
Important players are the UN, the World Trade Organization and the World Health Organization.
Non-governmental organisations and companies also play a part.
One example is the Paris Climate Agreement of 2015.
Geneva is one of the most important places for global governance.

abschnitte.text: The English word **governance** means steering or managing. Global governance means all the rules, treaties and organisations with which the world tackles shared problems. Unlike a country, the world has no **world government** and no world parliament. That is why countries have to agree on rules and work together voluntarily.

The most important players are the **countries** that make treaties. They are joined by international organisations such as the UN, the World Trade Organization WTO and the World Health Organization WHO. Meetings such as the G20 also belong to it. **Non-governmental organisations**, science and companies are becoming more and more important.

On climate protection, almost all countries committed themselves in the **Paris Climate Agreement** of 2015 to limiting global warming. The WTO sets rules for world trade, so that disputes are settled peacefully. With diseases such as COVID-19, the WHO coordinated information and recommendations. Protecting the ozone layer through the Montreal Protocol of 1987 is also seen as a successful example.

Alongside New York, Geneva is one of the most important places for international cooperation. The WHO, the WTO, the International Labour Organization and the ICRC, among others, have their seat here. The **Palais des Nations** houses the European seat of the UN. Switzerland calls this role **International Geneva** and supports it deliberately.

Global governance only works if countries keep to agreements. Often there are no penalties for countries that break rules. Critics complain that rich and powerful countries have more influence than poor countries. Others fear that countries give up too much **sovereignty** to international organisations.

begriffe.erklaerung: Steering or managing through rules and cooperation.
An organisation that is not run by the state, for example an aid organisation.
A country's right to decide its own affairs.
An association of countries with a shared aim.

gewusst: Thousands of people in Geneva work for international organisations.
The Montreal Protocol to protect the ozone layer has been ratified by all UN member states.
There is no world parliament in which people from all countries directly elect representatives.

teile.einleitung: The flag of Austria is red, white and red. It has three horizontal stripes and is one of the oldest flags in the world. Austria is Switzerland's neighbour to the east.
wichtigste: The Austrian flag is red and white.
It has three horizontal stripes: red, white, red.
The middle stripe is white.
A legend tells of a duke whose white tunic stayed white only under his belt.
The state flag also shows a black eagle.
Austria borders Switzerland to the east.

abschnitte.text: The flag of Austria has **three horizontal stripes**. **Red** is at the top and bottom, **white** in the middle. The three stripes are the same width. Austrians often simply say **“Rot-Weiss-Rot”** (red, white, red). These colours are among the **oldest national colours** in Europe.

A well-known **legend** tells how the colours came about. Long ago a duke is said to have fought in a **battle** on a crusade. Afterwards his **white tunic** was completely stained red. When he took off his **belt**, a **white stripe** was left underneath. This is said to be how red, white and red came about. Nobody knows whether it is true; it is a legend.

abschnitte.titel: The eagle in the coat of arms
abschnitte.text: Austria's **state flag** also shows the **national coat of arms** in the middle. It shows a **black eagle**. On its breast it carries a shield in red, white and red. This flag is used mainly by the authorities. Everyone may use the plain flag without the coat of arms.

Austria lies **east of Switzerland**. It borders the cantons of **St Gallen** and the **Grisons** and Liechtenstein. Part of the border runs along the **Rhine**, another part through the Alps. As in German-speaking Switzerland, people in Austria speak **German**. The capital is called **Vienna**.

gewusst: The flag of Latvia looks similar, but it is dark red and has a narrower white stripe.
Switzerland, Austria and Germany meet at Lake Constance.

teile.einleitung: Geopolitics studies how a country's location, size, raw materials and landscape influence its politics and its power. For example, it asks why straits, borders or mountain ranges are so important for countries. Many conflicts in the world can be understood better with geopolitical thinking.
wichtigste: Geopolitics combines geography and politics.
The term was coined around 1900 by the Swede Rudolf Kjellén.
In 1904 Halford Mackinder developed the Heartland Theory about the importance of Eurasia.
During the Cuban Missile Crisis in 1962, the USA and the Soviet Union stood on the brink of nuclear war.
India and Pakistan have been in dispute over the Kashmir region since 1947.
Since 1953 Switzerland has helped to monitor the ceasefire at the inter-Korean border.
Since 1974 the island of Cyprus has in practice been divided.

abschnitte.text: Geopolitics asks what part **geographical location** plays for countries. A country with access to the sea can trade more easily than a landlocked country such as Switzerland. Raw materials such as oil, gas or rare metals make regions important and fought over. **Straits** such as the Strait of Hormuz or canals such as the Suez Canal are also very important, because many ships pass through them.

Around 1900 the Swede **Rudolf Kjellén** coined the term geopolitics. In 1904 the Briton **Halford Mackinder** put forward the Heartland Theory: whoever controlled the heartland of Eurasia could control the world. In 1954 US President Eisenhower set out the **domino theory**, according to which neighbouring countries follow when one country becomes communist. In Germany, geopolitics was misused for plans of conquest in the Nazi period, which is why the word was disputed for a long time.

After 1945 the USA and the Soviet Union faced each other as superpowers. In 1962 the Soviet Union stationed nuclear missiles on Cuba, close to the USA, and the **Cuban Missile Crisis** followed. The world stood on the brink of nuclear war, but after 13 days both sides reached an agreement. Korea was also divided, and since the ceasefire of 1953 Switzerland has helped to monitor the border at Panmunjom.

India and Pakistan have been in dispute since 1947 over the **Kashmir** region in the Himalayas. Since 1974 the island of Cyprus has in practice been split into a Greek part and a Turkish part. The Bosnian War was ended in 1995 with the Dayton Agreement. For Western Sahara, the UN mission MINURSO has since 1991 been meant to prepare a referendum on its status, which has still not taken place.

In 1993 Israel and the PLO signed the first **Oslo Accord**, which was meant to start a peace process in the Middle East. Such agreements show that even difficult conflicts can be negotiated. Switzerland contributes with good offices and mediation. As a landlocked country without raw materials, it depends especially on stable relations and open trade routes.

begriffe.erklaerung: A narrow waterway between two land masses.
A country with very great military and economic power.
An agreement to stop fighting without peace having been made yet.
The heartland of Eurasia in Mackinder's theory.

gewusst: Swiss officers have been stationed at the border between North and South Korea for more than 70 years.
The Cuban Missile Crisis in October 1962 lasted about 13 days.
A large part of the oil traded worldwide is transported through the Strait of Hormuz.

teile.einleitung: Switzerland's good offices are an important part of Swiss foreign policy. Switzerland mediates between countries or represents countries that have no direct relations with each other. Because Switzerland is neutral, both sides of a conflict often trust it.
wichtigste: With its good offices, Switzerland mediates between countries or represents countries that have no direct relations.
A distinction is made between protecting power mandates, mediation and hosting negotiations.
Neutrality makes Switzerland a credible mediator.
Since 1980 Switzerland has represented the interests of the USA in Iran.
In the Second World War Switzerland had more than 200 protecting power mandates.
Geneva is a well-known place for peace talks and summits.

abschnitte.text: Good offices are forms of help that a neutral country offers so that other countries can talk to each other. Switzerland has been doing this for more than 150 years. It offers three kinds: **protecting power mandates**, mediation and acting as host. Switzerland does not force itself on anyone; it only helps when all sides agree.

When two countries break off diplomatic relations, a third country can step in as a **protecting power**. Switzerland then passes on messages and helps citizens of the country it represents. Since 1980 Switzerland has represented the interests of the USA in Iran. Since 2009 it has also had mandates for Russia in Georgia and for Georgia in Russia.

In **mediation**, Switzerland helps parties to a conflict to find a solution. Swiss diplomats have taken part, for example, in peace processes in Colombia, Mozambique or Nepal. They organise talks, contribute ideas and build trust. It is important that Switzerland stays **neutral** and does not favour anyone.

Switzerland often provides places for difficult negotiations. In 1962 the Algerian War was ended in Évian in France, in close cooperation with Switzerland. In 1985 US President Reagan and the Soviet leader Gorbachev met in **Geneva**. In 2021 a summit between Presidents Biden and Putin took place in Geneva.

Switzerland's **neutrality** is the most important reason why many countries trust it. In addition there is Geneva with its many international organisations, good security and experienced diplomats. The Federal Department of Foreign Affairs (**FDFA**) is responsible for good offices. In the Second World War, Switzerland at times held more than 200 mandates for about 35 countries.

begriffe.erklaerung: A country that represents the interests of another country in a third country.
Helping people in a dispute to find a solution themselves.
Looking after relations between countries through talks and treaties.
Switzerland's foreign ministry.

gewusst: For more than 45 years Switzerland has been the mouthpiece of the USA in Iran.
In the Second World War Switzerland held more than 200 protecting power mandates.
The 1985 summit of Reagan and Gorbachev in Geneva is seen as the beginning of the end of the Cold War.

teile.einleitung: The Gini coefficient is a number that shows how equally or unequally something is distributed. It is mostly used for income or wealth in a country. It always lies between 0 and 1.
wichtigste: The Gini coefficient measures the inequality of a distribution.
It is named after the Italian statistician Corrado Gini, who presented it in 1912.
0 means perfect equality; 1 means that one person owns everything.
It is derived from the Lorenz curve.
Taxes and social transfers lower the Gini coefficient of incomes.
In Switzerland, wealth is distributed much more unequally than income.

abschnitte.text: The **Gini coefficient** is a statistical measure of **unequal distribution**. At a value of **0**, everyone has exactly the same amount. At a value of **1**, everything belongs to a single person. The higher the value, the more unequal the distribution. Sometimes it is also given as a percentage, in which case it goes from 0 to 100.

The measure is named after the Italian statistician **Corrado Gini**. He presented it in **1912**. Gini studied population and distribution. Today statistical offices and organisations such as the **World Bank** and the **OECD** use his coefficient to compare countries. In Switzerland, the Federal Statistical Office publishes such values.

The Gini coefficient is derived from the **Lorenz curve**. It shows what share of the population has what share of the income. With complete equality it would be a straight line, the **line of equality**. The area between this line and the Lorenz curve is called A, and the area under the curve B. The Gini coefficient is **A divided by A plus B**. Example: 0.15 divided by 0.5 gives 0.3.

A distinction is made between **market incomes**, meaning wages and income from capital, and **disposable incomes** after taxes and social benefits. **Progressive taxes** and transfers such as **AVS pensions** or social assistance redistribute income. That is why the Gini coefficient of disposable incomes is lower than that of market incomes. How much should be redistributed is disputed in politics.

In **Switzerland** the Gini coefficient of disposable incomes is about **0.3**. The Gini coefficient of **wealth** is clearly higher. Wealth is often passed down over generations and grows through income from capital. According to the World Bank, **South Africa**, with values above 0.6, is one of the countries with the most unequal distribution of income. The effects of apartheid are still felt there today.

gewusst: Two countries can have the same Gini value even though their distributions look completely different.
The Gini coefficient says nothing about whether a country is rich or poor.

t1q3k042.t: Flag of the People's Republic of China

teile.einleitung: The flag of the People's Republic of China is red and shows five yellow stars in the top left: one large and four small. It has been used since the founding of the People's Republic in 1949. In Chinese its name means roughly “Five-Star Red Flag”.
wichtigste: China's flag has a red background.
In the top left there are five yellow stars.
There is one large star with four small ones in an arc beside it.
The large star stands for the Communist Party, the small ones for the people.
The red stands for the communist revolution.
The flag has been used since 1 October 1949.

abschnitte.text: China's flag has a **red background**. In the top left corner there are **five yellow stars**. There is **one large star** and **four small stars**, which stand in an arc beside it. Each small star points one of its tips towards the large star. The rest of the flag is simply red.

The **red** stands for the **communist revolution**. In China, red has also long been seen as a **lucky colour**. The **large star** stands for the **Communist Party**, which governs the country. The **four small stars** stand for the **people**. Originally they meant four groups of the population, such as workers and farmers.

The **People's Republic of China** was founded on **1 October 1949**. At that time a long civil war ended. The Communist Party under **Mao Zedong** took power. The red flag with the five stars has been used since that day. Today 1 October is China's **National Day**.

The flag was raised ceremonially for the first time in **Beijing**, in **Tiananmen Square** (the Square of the Gate of Heavenly Peace). Beijing is the **capital** of China. To this day the flag is raised there every morning at sunrise. Many visitors watch.

gewusst: The flag was chosen from thousands of designs sent in after a public appeal.
China is one of the countries with the largest population in the world.

teile.einleitung: The General Assembly is the body of the United Nations in which all member countries are represented. It is something like a large parliament of the world. It meets at the UN headquarters in New York.
wichtigste: All 193 member countries of the UN sit in the General Assembly.
Each country has one vote.
The main session begins every September in New York.
In the General Debate, heads of state give their speeches.
Most decisions are recommendations without legal force.
The General Assembly decides the UN's budget.
In 2015 it adopted 17 Sustainable Development Goals.

abschnitte.text: All **193 member countries** of the UN are represented in the **General Assembly**. Each country has **one vote**, whether it is large or small. The Assembly meets in the great hall at the **UN headquarters in New York**. Behind the speaker's lectern is a large **golden wall** with the UN emblem, which you often see on television.

Every year in **September** the main session begins. Then many presidents and heads of government travel to New York. In the **General Debate**, each country speaks to the Assembly. The General Assembly also elects a new **President** every year. In this way countries from different world regions take their turn.

Most decisions, the **resolutions**, are **recommendations**. They are not legally binding on the countries. Certain decisions of the **Security Council**, on the other hand, are binding. Even so, resolutions of the General Assembly carry great political weight, because almost all the countries of the world have a say. The General Assembly also decides the UN's **budget** and lays down how much each country pays.

In 2015 the General Assembly adopted **17 Sustainable Development Goals**. They aim, for example, to reduce **hunger** and **poverty** by 2030, give more children an education and protect the climate. These goals also apply to Switzerland.

Switzerland only joined the UN in 2002, after the people and the cantons had said yes in a vote. This made it the 190th member. From 2010 to 2011 the former Federal Councillor **Joseph Deiss** chaired the General Assembly as its President. Geneva is also home to the UN's most important seat in Europe.

gewusst: Joining the UN was decided on 3 March 2002; an earlier proposal had been clearly rejected in 1986.
The General Assembly can only admit new members on the recommendation of the Security Council.

t1r57whe.t: Global Compact for Safe, Orderly and Regular Migration

teile.einleitung: The Global Compact for Safe, Orderly and Regular Migration is a UN agreement. It contains shared principles and goals for dealing with migration, meaning people who leave their country to live somewhere else. It is often called the Global Compact for Migration.
wichtigste: The Migration Compact is an international agreement with shared principles for dealing with migration.
It was adopted in Marrakesh in Morocco in December 2018.
The Compact is not legally binding.
It contains 23 goals, for example less people smuggling and better data.
A Swiss diplomat led the negotiations together with Mexico.
Switzerland has not yet agreed to the Compact.

abschnitte.text: **Migration** means that people move to another place permanently, for example because of work, family or hardship. Around the world, about 280 million people do not live in the country where they were born (as of about 2020). The Migration Compact is meant to help migration happen more safely and in a more orderly way. It is a **framework** for cooperation between countries, not a law.

In 2016 the UN member states decided in the New York Declaration to draw up two compacts. The negotiations on the Migration Compact were led by the Swiss ambassador **Jürg Lauber**, together with a diplomat from Mexico. In December 2018 the Compact was adopted at a conference in **Marrakesh**. Shortly afterwards the UN General Assembly confirmed it with a large majority.

The Compact contains **23 goals**. They include better data on migration, the fight against people smugglers and human trafficking, and saving lives on dangerous routes. Migrants should have identity papers and enjoy basic rights. Returning home and tackling the causes of migration are also topics.

The Compact is **not legally binding**; each country decides its own migration policy. Even so, it was disputed in many countries. Some countries, such as the USA and Hungary, rejected it. Supporters see it as an important step towards cooperation; opponents feared it could restrict their own policies.

Although a Swiss diplomat had led the negotiations, Switzerland did not take part in the conference in Marrakesh in 2018. The **Federal Council** wanted to involve Parliament first, because the topic was highly disputed at home. To this day Switzerland has not agreed to the Compact. Alongside it there is the **Global Compact on Refugees**, which concerns people who have fled and which Switzerland supports.

begriffe.erklaerung: People moving permanently to another area or country.
An agreement between several partners.
When a treaty must be kept and can be enforced in court.
Someone who takes people across borders illegally for money.

gewusst: The Migration Compact was the first worldwide UN text to deal with migration comprehensively.
A Swiss ambassador led the negotiations, but Switzerland itself has not adopted the Compact.
At the UN, refugees and migrants are dealt with in two different compacts.

teile.einleitung: France is Switzerland's western neighbour and one of the largest countries in Europe. Its capital, Paris, is famous for the Eiffel Tower and the Louvre. France shares the Jura, Lake Geneva and the French language with Switzerland.
wichtigste: France lies to the west of Switzerland.
The capital, Paris, lies on the Seine.
The Eiffel Tower was built in 1889 for a world's fair.
The Mona Lisa by Leonardo da Vinci hangs in the Louvre.
The canton of Geneva is almost completely surrounded by France.
The Tour de France has existed since 1903.

abschnitte.text: The capital of France is **Paris**. The **Seine** flows through the middle of the city, crossed by many beautiful bridges. The landmark of Paris is the **Eiffel Tower**. It was built in **1889** for a **world's fair**, is made of **iron** and today is over **300 metres** tall. The **Mona Lisa** by **Leonardo da Vinci** hangs in the **Louvre**, one of the largest museums in the world.

France lies **west of Switzerland**. The cantons of **Geneva**, **Vaud**, **Neuchâtel**, **Jura**, **Solothurn** and **Basel** border on France, as do parts of the Valais. The canton of **Geneva** is almost completely surrounded by France. Only a small stretch borders the canton of Vaud. In **French-speaking Switzerland**, the Romandy, people speak **French**, as in France.

On the border with Switzerland lies the **Jura**, a long mountain range between Geneva and Basel. The two countries share **Lake Geneva**: the north shore belongs to Switzerland, and the south shore mostly to France. In French it is called **“Lac Léman”**. On the border between France and Italy stands **Mont Blanc**. It is about **4,800 metres** high and the **highest mountain in the Alps**.

France is famous for its **food**. A typical example is the **baguette**, a long, thin white loaf with a crunchy crust. Many people buy it fresh at the bakery every day. Hundreds of kinds of **cheese** and fine pastries such as the croissant are also well known. The French language is also spoken in many countries around the world.

Every summer the **Tour de France** takes place. It is the most famous **cycle race** in the world and has been held since **1903**. The riders are on the road for about **three weeks** and also ride over high passes in the Alps and the Pyrenees. Whoever is fastest overall wears the **yellow jersey**. Now and then a stage even passes through Switzerland.

gewusst: By area, France is the largest country in the European Union.
In 2022 the baguette was added to UNESCO's list of intangible cultural heritage.

teile.einleitung: The Loss and Damage Fund is meant to help countries that suffer especially badly from the effects of climate change. It was agreed in 2022 at the COP27 climate conference in Egypt. It covers damage that can no longer be prevented despite adaptation.
wichtigste: The fund was agreed in 2022 at COP27 in Sharm el-Sheikh.
Loss and damage are climate effects that happen despite adaptation.
During a transitional phase, the World Bank manages the fund as trustee.
The board has its seat in the Philippines.
Since 2013 the Warsaw Mechanism has dealt with the issue.
Article 8 of the Paris Agreement deals with loss and damage.

abschnitte.text: In climate protection there are three big areas. **Mitigation** means emitting fewer greenhouse gases. **Adaptation** means preparing for the effects, for example with dams. **Loss and damage** are effects that happen **despite adaptation**. Examples are severe **storms**, long **droughts** or the **rise in sea level**, which threatens whole coastlines.

Some damage can be measured in money. This includes destroyed houses, roads or **crop failures**. It is called **economic** damage. Other losses can hardly be expressed in money. These are **non-economic** losses, for example the loss of **cultural heritage**, **home**, identity or **biodiversity**.

Since **2013** the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change has had the **Warsaw Mechanism**. It was created at **COP19** in Poland and promotes knowledge and cooperation, but it does not hand out any money itself. In the **Paris Agreement** of 2015, **Article 8** deals with loss and damage. According to an accompanying decision, however, it does not create any **liability** or duty to pay compensation. For a long time many **developing countries** demanded a fund of its own.

At **COP27** in **Sharm el-Sheikh** in Egypt, the countries decided in **2022** to create the fund. A **transitional committee** then worked out the details. For the first **four years**, the fund is based at the **World Bank**, which manages it as trustee. Developing countries had criticised this solution at first. In **2024** the **Philippines** was chosen as the host country of the board. The country is hit especially hard by **typhoons**.

There is a lot of debate about the fund. One question is **who should pay in** and how much. Countries that have emitted a lot of greenhouse gases see their duty differently from countries that have hardly contributed. Another question is how the money can reach those affected **quickly and fairly**. Switzerland also takes part in these international negotiations.

gewusst: Small island states in the Pacific are among the countries most threatened by the rise in sea level.
The abbreviation COP stands for “Conference of the Parties”.

t1t9n9p4.t: Free trade agreement between Switzerland and the EEC

teile.einleitung: The free trade agreement of 1972 is one of the most important treaties between Switzerland and today's European Union. It makes sure that industrial goods such as machines, watches or medicines can be traded across the border without customs duties. Many Swiss companies still benefit from it today.
wichtigste: The agreement was concluded in 1972 between Switzerland and the European Economic Community (EEC).
It came into force on 1 January 1973.
It allows duty-free trade in industrial goods.
Farm products are mostly not included.
Swiss voters clearly approved the agreement in December 1972.
The EU is still Switzerland's most important trading partner today.

abschnitte.text: A **free trade agreement** is a treaty in which countries agree to do without customs duties and quantity limits. The 1972 agreement applies to **industrial goods**, meaning goods made in factories such as machines, chemicals, watches or textiles. For farm products such as cheese or meat, on the other hand, there are separate rules. The agreement is one of the foundations of relations between Switzerland and the EU.

In 1957 six countries founded the **European Economic Community**, EEC for short. Switzerland did not join it, but in 1960 it founded **EFTA**, the European Free Trade Association, with other countries. When Great Britain and Denmark moved from EFTA to the EEC in 1973, the remaining EFTA countries wanted to secure access to the EEC market. That is why in 1972 the EEC concluded free trade agreements with several EFTA countries, including Switzerland.

In Switzerland the agreement was put to the people on 3 December 1972. About 72 per cent of voters said yes, and all the cantons agreed. This shows how important **exports** to Europe already were for Switzerland at that time. The agreement came into force on 1 January 1973.

Switzerland is a small country and sells a large part of its goods abroad. Without customs duties, Swiss products are cheaper in countries such as Germany, France or Italy, and so easier to sell. In the other direction, Swiss companies and customers can import goods from the EU duty-free. A large part of Switzerland's foreign trade is with the **EU**.

In 1992 the Swiss people narrowly rejected joining the European Economic Area (EEA). After that Switzerland relied on **bilateral agreements**, meaning individual agreements with the EU. The Bilaterals I came into force in 2002, and the Bilaterals II followed from 2005. The free trade agreement of 1972 always remained an important foundation.

begriffe.erklaerung: A charge you have to pay when goods are brought across a national border.
Trade between countries without customs duties and other obstacles.
The European Economic Community, a forerunner of today's EU.
The European Free Trade Association, which Switzerland has belonged to since 1960.
Agreements between two partners, here between Switzerland and the EU.

gewusst: The 1972 agreement has applied for more than 50 years and is still in use.
When it was founded in 1957, the EEC had only six members; today the EU has 27 member states.
In the 1972 vote, all the cantons said yes to the agreement.

teile.einleitung: Federalism means that power in a state is shared between several levels. In Switzerland, the Confederation, the 26 cantons and the municipalities share the tasks. This way decisions can often be made where people live.
wichtigste: Federalism shares state power between several levels.
Switzerland has three levels: Confederation, cantons and municipalities.
Since 1848 Switzerland has been a federal state with a shared Federal Constitution.
The cantons are responsible for all tasks that the Federal Constitution does not give to the Confederation.
According to the principle of subsidiarity, the higher level only takes on what the lower level cannot manage itself.
Since 2008 the new system of financial equalisation (NFA) has reduced the financial differences between the cantons.
Since 1 January 1979 the Jura has been Switzerland's youngest canton.

abschnitte.text: The word comes from the Latin **foedus**, which means alliance. In a federal state, the member states have their own rights, their own governments and their own laws. At the same time there is a shared overall state that takes on important tasks for everyone. The opposite is a **centralised state** such as France, where a lot is decided in the capital.

abschnitte.titel: From confederation of states to federal state
abschnitte.text: For a long time the old Swiss Confederacy was a **confederation of states**: the members remained fully sovereign and had only loose treaties with each other. After the Sonderbund War of 1847, the cantons gave themselves a shared Federal Constitution in 1848. This made Switzerland a **federal state** with a Federal Council, a parliament and Bern as its capital. The Confederation was given tasks such as the army, the post and the coinage.

The **Confederation** looks after things such as foreign policy, the army, the railways and the national roads. The **cantons** are responsible for, among other things, schools, the police and hospitals; that is why school systems and holidays are not the same everywhere. The roughly 2,100 municipalities (as of about 2025) deal with things such as rubbish, water and local planning. Every canton has its own constitution, its own parliament and its own government.

The **principle of subsidiarity** says that a task should be done as close to the people as possible. Only when the municipality or the canton cannot manage something alone does the higher level help. The cantons also have a say at federal level, for example in the **Council of States**, where every full canton has two seats. Changes to the Constitution also need the majority of the cantons. Since 1993 the **Conference of Cantonal Governments** has represented the shared interests of the cantons towards the Confederation.

Not all cantons are equally rich; Zug or Basel-Stadt have much higher tax revenues than, say, Uri or the Jura. That is why since 2008 there has been the **new system of financial equalisation**, NFA for short. Financially strong cantons and the Confederation pay money to financially weaker cantons. This way all the cantons can carry out their tasks well without losing their independence.

Other countries are also organised federally. Germany has 16 federal states, Austria 9 federal states and the USA 50 states. Federalism helps especially in countries with different languages and cultures, such as Switzerland with its four national languages. Critics say that it is sometimes complicated and slow; supporters praise its closeness to the people and the **competition** of good ideas.

begriffe.erklaerung: A state made up of member states that have their own rights but together form an overall state.
A loose association in which the members remain fully independent.
Tasks are carried out as far as possible by the lower level, closest to the citizens.
The majority of the cantons, which is needed in votes on the Constitution.
Money is redistributed between rich and poorer cantons.

gewusst: The canton of Jura was created in 1979 by separating from the canton of Bern and is the youngest canton.
Because the cantons are responsible for schools, the summer holidays do not start at the same time everywhere.
Six cantons, for example Appenzell Innerrhoden, have only one seat in the Council of States, because they used to be counted as half-cantons.

teile.einleitung: The United Nations peacekeeping forces are soldiers, police officers and civilian experts who keep the peace in crisis areas on behalf of the UN. Because of their light blue helmets and caps, they are called Blue Helmets. For example, they monitor ceasefires and protect the population.
wichtigste: Soldiers serving on behalf of the UN are called Blue Helmets.
The first UN peacekeeping mission began in the Middle East in 1948.
The Blue Helmets are provided by member states; the UN has no army of its own.
The UN Security Council decides on new missions.
In 1988 the peacekeeping forces received the Nobel Peace Prize.
Switzerland sends unarmed military observers and experts on UN missions.

abschnitte.text: Blue Helmets are members of armies and police forces from many countries who serve under the UN flag for a time. Their sign of recognition is the **light blue helmets** or berets with the UN emblem. A mission also includes civilian experts, for example for human rights, elections or clearing mines. The UN has no army of its own, so the **member states** provide the troops.

Blue Helmets monitor **ceasefires** and borders between parties to a conflict. They protect civilians, help to disarm fighters and support elections. Often they make sure that aid organisations can work safely. Normally they may only use weapons in self-defence or to protect people.

The first peacekeeping mission, **UNTSO**, began in the Middle East in 1948 and still exists today. In 1956, during the Suez Crisis, the first armed force was sent. Since then there have been more than 70 missions, for example in Cyprus, Lebanon, the Congo or South Sudan. In 1988 the United Nations peacekeeping forces jointly received the **Nobel Peace Prize**.

The UN **Security Council** in New York decides on a new mission. Usually the parties to the conflict must agree to the Blue Helmets coming. The mission is given a mandate that lays down exactly what it may do. It is paid for from a special budget to which all member states contribute.

In 1994 Swiss voters rejected creating Swiss armed Blue Helmet troops. But since 1990 Switzerland has sent unarmed **military observers** on UN missions, for example to the Middle East. Experts in mine clearance and police officers also serve. In addition, since 1999 the Swiss Army has carried out a peace mission in Kosovo with **Swisscoy**, which is based on a UN mandate.

begriffe.erklaerung: A task that lays down exactly what a mission may do.
An agreement to stop fighting for the time being.
The UN body that decides on questions of war and peace.
Unarmed officers who watch whether agreements are being kept.

gewusst: The very first UN peacekeeping mission of 1948 is still in operation today.
The International Day of UN Peacekeepers is marked every year on 29 May.
In 1988 the Blue Helmets received the Nobel Peace Prize as a group.

teile.einleitung: Liechtenstein is a small neighbour of Switzerland and a principality. Its head of state is the prince from the Liechtenstein family. Since 1989 this has been Prince Hans-Adam II (as of 2026).
wichtigste: Liechtenstein is a principality; the head of state is the prince.
Prince Hans-Adam II has been in office since 1989 (as of 2026).
Since 2004 Hereditary Prince Alois has carried out most official business as his deputy.
The princely family lives in Vaduz Castle.
The national holiday is on 15 August.
The country is named after the princely family.

abschnitte.titel: A prince as head of state
abschnitte.text: Liechtenstein is a **monarchy**: the office of head of state is passed down in the family. At the same time Liechtenstein is a **democracy**, with an elected parliament, the Landtag, and popular votes. The prince and the people share power. For example, a law also needs the prince's approval.

Since 1989 **Hans-Adam II** has been Prince of Liechtenstein (as of 2026). His son **Alois** is the **Hereditary Prince**, meaning the heir to the throne. In 2004 the prince made him his **deputy**. Since then Hereditary Prince Alois has carried out most of the official business. Later he will take over the office of prince.

abschnitte.titel: Vaduz Castle and the national holiday
abschnitte.text: The princely family lives in **Vaduz Castle**, which stands high above the capital. Because it is a home, you cannot visit it. On **15 August** Liechtenstein celebrates its **national holiday**. On that day the princely family invites the population into the castle garden.

The country is named after the **princely family**. The family bought the territory about 300 years ago but lived in Austria for a long time. In **Vienna** it still owns the **Garden Palace** and the **City Palace Liechtenstein**. There it shows paintings from its large art collection.

gewusst: In Liechtenstein people pay with the Swiss franc.
Since 1924 Liechtenstein and Switzerland have formed a shared customs area.

teile.einleitung: The flag of Germany shows three horizontal stripes in black, red and gold. It is officially called the federal flag, because Germany is a federal state. Its colours have a long history connected with the wish for unity and freedom.
wichtigste: The German flag has three horizontal stripes of equal width.
Black is at the top, red in the middle and gold at the bottom.
The colour gold looks like a strong yellow.
The national flag is officially called the federal flag.
The federal service flag used by the authorities also shows the federal eagle.
Germany is Switzerland's northern neighbour.

abschnitte.text: The federal flag is made up of three **horizontal stripes** of equal width. **Black** is at the top, **red** in the middle and **gold** at the bottom. Gold is the official name here for a strong yellow. The Basic Law, Germany's constitution, contains the sentence: “The federal flag shall be black, red and gold.” The flag is a rectangle that is wider than it is tall.

Besides the plain federal flag there is the **federal service flag**. It is used by federal authorities, for example ministries. In its middle is the **federal coat of arms** with the **federal eagle**. The eagle is black and has a red beak and red claws. Ordinary citizens may not simply use this service flag.

The colours black, red and gold became well known in the **19th century**. At that time Germany was made up of many small states. Many people wanted a **united country** with more freedom and more say. At large gatherings and in the **Revolution of 1848** they showed flags in these colours. Later the colours became the country's flag.

After the Second World War, Germany was divided into two states. The **Federal Republic** in the west used the black, red and gold flag from **1949**. The **GDR** in the east had the same colours, but with its own emblem in the middle. Since **reunification in 1990** there has again been only one German flag.

Germany lies **north of Switzerland**. For the most part the border runs along the **Rhine** and **Lake Constance**. Cantons such as Basel-Stadt, Schaffhausen or Thurgau border on Germany. Many people commute across this border to work every day. That is why you quite often see the black, red and gold flag in Switzerland too.

gewusst: Belgium has the same three colours, but with vertical stripes and yellow instead of gold.
The sentence about the federal flag is in Article 22 of the Basic Law.
The federal eagle is sometimes affectionately called the “fat hen”, because one version in the Bundestag looks very round.

teile.einleitung: Shaking hands is one of the best-known greetings in the world. People shake hands to say hello, to say goodbye or after reaching an agreement. In politics too, a handshake is an important sign.
wichtigste: People usually shake with their right hand.
In Switzerland people often greet each other with a handshake.
After negotiations, a handshake shows that people are in agreement.
An old explanation says that an open hand shows you are not carrying a weapon.
During the coronavirus period, many people greeted each other with their elbows.
In Japan people traditionally bow to greet each other.

abschnitte.text: **Shaking hands** is very old. A well-known explanation says that anyone who offers an **open hand** shows that they are **not carrying a weapon**. This builds trust. Nobody knows for certain whether this is really the origin. Today people usually shake with their **right hand**. This is an old habit.

In Switzerland people often greet each other with a **handshake**, for example at work or when meeting someone for the first time. People sometimes shake hands when saying goodbye too. With a polite handshake you look the other person **in the eye**. This shows openness and respect. The grip should be neither too firm nor too limp.

When politicians shake hands after negotiations, it shows that they have **reached an agreement**. Such moments are often photographed and go round the world. A famous example is the handshake between the Israeli Prime Minister **Yitzhak Rabin** and the Palestinian leader **Yasser Arafat** in Washington in 1993. It stood for the hope of peace.

After a game, athletes often shake hands. This is a sign of **fairness** and **respect**, no matter who has won. In tennis the players meet at the net after the last point. In football the teams shake hands before kick-off.

People do not shake hands everywhere. In **Japan** people traditionally bow. The deeper the **bow**, the more respect you show. During the **coronavirus period**, people wanted to avoid infections. That is why many greeted each other with their **elbows** or simply waved.

gewusst: The handshake between Rabin and Arafat took place in front of the White House, with US President Bill Clinton present.
In spring 2020 the Confederation also recommended not shaking hands.

teile.einleitung: From 1932 to 1934 a large conference took place in Geneva, at which countries negotiated about having fewer weapons. It had been called by the League of Nations, the forerunner of the UN. But the conference failed.
wichtigste: The conference took place in Geneva from 1932 to 1934.
The League of Nations had called it.
About 4,000 people from 64 countries took part.
Germany left the conference on 14 October 1933.
No disarmament agreement was reached.

abschnitte.titel: A conference of the League of Nations
abschnitte.text: After the First World War, many countries wanted to prevent another war on such a scale. The **League of Nations**, with its seat in **Geneva**, was meant to secure peace. In 1932 it called a large **disarmament conference**. **Disarmament** means that countries reduce their weapons and armies. About 4,000 people from 64 countries took part.

The countries found it hard to agree. Germany demanded to be allowed as many weapons as the other great powers. After the National Socialists came to power, **Germany** left the conference on **14 October 1933**. A few days later it also gave up its membership of the **League of Nations**. After that no agreement was reached.

The failure of the conference showed how weak the League of Nations was. A few years later the **Second World War** began. But Geneva remained an important place for talks about weapons. To this day countries negotiate there within the UN on **disarmament** and arms control.

gewusst: The Briton Arthur Henderson chaired the conference and received the Nobel Peace Prize in 1934.

teile.einleitung: The flag of Spain has three horizontal stripes in red, yellow and red. The yellow stripe in the middle is twice as wide as each red one. The state flag also carries the coat of arms of Spain with a crown and two pillars.
wichtigste: The Spanish flag is red and yellow and has three horizontal stripes.
The yellow stripe is twice as wide as each red one.
The flag is often called the “Rojigualda”, after its colours.
Near the flagpole, the coat of arms of Spain stands on the yellow.
The coat of arms has two pillars with the motto “Plus Ultra”.
At the top the coat of arms has a crown, and at the bottom it shows a pomegranate.

abschnitte.text: The flag of Spain has **three horizontal stripes**. **Red** is at the top and bottom, **yellow** in the middle. The **yellow stripe** is **twice as wide** as each of the two red ones. Many people call the flag the **“Rojigualda”**. The word is made up of “rojo” for red and “gualda” for a strong yellow.

The red and yellow flag goes back to the **18th century**. At that time many kingdoms in Europe had similar, often white flags. At sea it was hard to tell the ships apart. That is why the Spanish king had a new, easily visible flag in **red and yellow** designed for the fleet. Later it became the flag of the whole country.

On the state flag, the **coat of arms of Spain** stands near the flagpole. At the top is a **royal crown**, because Spain is a **kingdom**. The shield shows the signs of old kingdoms, for example a **castle** for Castile and a **lion** for León. Right at the bottom is a **pomegranate**. It stands for **Granada**, because “granada” means pomegranate in Spanish.

To the left and right of the shield stand **two pillars**. They recall the **Pillars of Hercules**, the name given in ancient times to the rocks at the **Strait of Gibraltar**. Ribbons with the words **“Plus Ultra”** wind round the pillars. This is Latin and means **“further beyond”**. The motto recalls that Spanish seafarers sailed far beyond the Mediterranean.

gewusst: At many events in Spain a simple version of the flag without the coat of arms is also used.
The pillars with the ribbons are seen as one possible origin of the dollar sign.

teile.einleitung: The Arctic around the North Pole is becoming more and more important for world politics. Because the ice is melting, shipping routes and raw materials are becoming easier to reach. That is why several countries are arguing about rights and influence in the far north.
wichtigste: The Arctic Council was founded in 1996 and has eight member states.
Switzerland has been an observer in the Arctic Council since 2017.
Russia, Denmark and Canada claim the Lomonosov Ridge under the North Pole.
In 2007 a Russian expedition placed a titanium flag on the seabed at the North Pole.
Since 2018 China has called itself a “near-Arctic state”.
The Arctic is warming almost four times as fast as the global average.

abschnitte.text: The **Arctic Council** was founded in 1996. Its members are the eight countries **Denmark**, **Finland**, **Iceland**, **Canada**, **Norway**, **Russia**, **Sweden** and the **USA**. In addition, organisations of **Indigenous peoples** are represented as permanent participants. Indigenous peoples are the original inhabitants of an area. **Switzerland** has been an observer since 2017 and explains its interest with its polar and glacier research.

According to a study from 2022, the Arctic has warmed **almost four times as fast** as the global average since 1979. The **sea ice** is shrinking. As a result, **shipping routes** can be used for longer in summer, and **raw materials** such as oil and gas are easier to reach. This increases the competition between countries.

Under the North Pole runs the **Lomonosov Ridge**, an underwater mountain range. **Russia**, **Denmark** and **Canada** regard it as an extension of their **continental shelf**. Whoever gets this recognised can claim rights to the seabed. In 2007 a Russian diving expedition led by Artur Chilingarov placed a **titanium flag** on the seabed. The action was symbolic and has no legal effect.

Canada and the USA are in dispute over the **Northwest Passage**. Canada sees it as its own internal waters, while the USA sees it as an international strait with free passage. In the north-west of **Greenland** is **Pituffik Space Base**, which was called Thule Air Base until 2023. It is used for early warning of missiles. Greenland belongs to the Kingdom of **Denmark** and is strategically important.

Countries outside the Arctic also want a say. **China** does not lie on the Arctic Ocean, but in its white paper of 2018 it calls itself a **“near-Arctic state”**. In it China also speaks of a **“Polar Silk Road”**, meaning new trade routes through the Arctic. After Russia's attack on Ukraine in 2022, the other seven members temporarily suspended cooperation with Russia in the Arctic Council.

gewusst: The Arctic Council does not deal with military questions.
The North Pole itself lies in the middle of the sea, not on solid land.

t1yyr7fe.t: High Representative for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy

teile.einleitung: The High Representative of the Union for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy is something like the foreign minister of the European Union. They represent the EU towards other countries. The present post has existed since the Treaty of Lisbon.
wichtigste: The present post was created by the Treaty of Lisbon, which came into force in 2009.
The High Representative is also Vice-President of the European Commission.
The European External Action Service (EEAS) reports to them.
They are appointed by the European Council by qualified majority.
Since 1 December 2024 Kaja Kallas has held the post (as of 2026).
Before her, Catherine Ashton, Federica Mogherini and Josep Borrell held the post.

abschnitte.text: From 1999 to 2009 there was already a **High Representative for the Common Foreign and Security Policy** (CFSP). This post was held by the Spaniard **Javier Solana**, previously NATO Secretary General. The **Treaty of Lisbon** of 2009 merged this post with that of the **Commissioner for External Relations**. This created today's post of High Representative.

The High Representative has two tasks. They lead foreign policy among the member states and are at the same time **Vice-President of the European Commission**. That is why people speak of the **double hat**. They also chair the meetings of the EU's foreign ministers. This is meant to let the EU speak with one voice to the outside world.

The **European External Action Service**, **EEAS** for short, reports to the High Representative. It is the EU's diplomatic service. It began work in 2011. The EEAS runs more than 140 **delegations** around the world, similar to embassies. One of them is in **Bern**. It looks after relations between the EU and Switzerland.

Under Article 18 of the EU Treaty, the **European Council** appoints the High Representative by qualified majority. The President of the Commission must agree. As a member of the Commission, the High Representative must also be confirmed by the **European Parliament**. The first holder of the post was the Briton **Catherine Ashton** (2009 to 2014). She was followed by Federica Mogherini and **Josep Borrell** (2019 to 2024). Since December 2024 the former Estonian head of government **Kaja Kallas** has held the post.

gewusst: Before taking up the post, Josep Borrell had been President of the European Parliament.
Before taking up the post, Catherine Ashton had been EU Trade Commissioner.

teile.einleitung: The flag of the United Nations is mainly light blue and shows a white emblem with a map of the world in the middle. It stands for the UN, which works for peace and cooperation around the world. You can see it, for example, in front of the UN headquarters in Geneva or on peacekeeping missions of the Blue Helmets.
wichtigste: The flag of the United Nations is mainly light blue.
In the middle is a white emblem with a map of the world.
The map of the world is surrounded by two olive branches.
The olive branches are a sign of peace.
The flag was officially adopted in 1947.
Switzerland has been a member of the UN since 2002.

abschnitte.text: The **UN flag** has a light blue background. In the middle is the white **emblem** of the United Nations. It shows a map of the world seen from the North Pole, with circles and lines like a grid of latitude and longitude. Around the map are two **olive branches**.

Since ancient times, olive branches have been seen as a sign of **peace**. The map of the world shows that the UN wants to be there for everyone on Earth. Because the map is drawn from the North Pole, no country and no continent is at the centre. The light blue is meant to give a sense of calm and peace, unlike red, which is often linked with war.

The United Nations was founded in 1945 after the Second World War. The **emblem** was fixed in 1946, and the flag was adopted by the General Assembly on 20 October 1947. The idea for the emblem came from a team led by the architect Oliver Lincoln Lundquist. Since then the flag has become known around the world.

On peacekeeping missions, UN soldiers wear blue helmets or caps. That is why they are called **Blue Helmets**. Their vehicles are usually white and carry the letters UN. They are meant to help monitor ceasefires and protect the population.

Switzerland joined the UN after a popular vote on 3 March 2002. In **Geneva**, the Palais des Nations is the second-largest seat of the UN after New York. There the UN flag flies together with the flags of all the member states. Many UN organisations, such as the refugee agency UNHCR, have their seat in Geneva.

begriffe.erklaerung: A picture sign that stands for an organisation.
A branch of the olive tree, which has long been a sign of peace.
UN soldiers who help on peacekeeping missions.
The UN, an organisation of almost all the countries in the world for peace and cooperation.

gewusst: The colour of the UN flag is often called UN blue and is a shade of its own.
The map of the world on the UN emblem does not show Antarctica.
The UN has 193 member states, and in front of the headquarters in New York a flag flies for each of them.

teile.einleitung: The Gaza war began on 7 October 2023 with a major attack by Hamas on Israel. After that Israel waged a war in the Gaza Strip. The war has claimed a very large number of victims and is highly disputed politically.
wichtigste: On 7 October 2023 armed fighters of Hamas and other groups attacked Israel.
About 1,200 people were killed and about 250 were taken away as hostages.
Hamas has controlled the Gaza Strip alone since 2007.
Before the war about 2 million people lived in the Gaza Strip.
Qatar, Egypt and the USA mediated between Israel and Hamas.
South Africa brought a case against Israel at the International Court of Justice.
In 2024 the International Criminal Court issued arrest warrants against Israeli politicians and a Hamas leader.

abschnitte.text: The **Gaza Strip** is a narrow area on the Mediterranean between Israel and Egypt. Before the war about **2 million people** lived on only about 360 square kilometres. It is one of the most densely populated areas in the world. **Hamas** won the Palestinian parliamentary elections in 2006 and drove out Fatah by force in 2007. Since then Hamas has governed in Gaza and the **Palestinian Authority** in the West Bank.

On 7 October 2023 armed fighters of Hamas and other groups broke into **Israel** from the Gaza Strip. About **1,200 people** were killed, most of them civilians, including many people at a music festival. About **250 people** were taken to Gaza as **hostages**. It was the day on which more Jews were killed than on any day since the Holocaust.

Israel responded with air strikes and a ground offensive in the Gaza Strip. The aim was to destroy Hamas and free the hostages. In the war, **tens of thousands of people** were killed in Gaza, and a great many buildings were destroyed. Almost the whole population had to flee, and there was a shortage of food, water and medicines. The **Rafah** border crossing to Egypt was important for aid deliveries.

Israel and Hamas do not negotiate directly with each other. That is why **Qatar**, **Egypt** and the **USA** mediated. There were several **truces**, during which hostages were exchanged for Palestinian prisoners. Many countries and aid organisations called for more humanitarian aid for Gaza. Switzerland supported aid for the civilian population and called on all sides to respect international law.

In December 2023 **South Africa** brought a case of genocide against Israel at the **International Court of Justice** in The Hague. Israel rejects the accusation. In 2024 the court ordered provisional measures; a judgment was still pending (as of 2025). In November 2024 the **International Criminal Court** issued arrest warrants for war crimes against **Benjamin Netanyahu** and **Yoav Gallant**. An arrest warrant was also issued against the Hamas military leader Mohammed Deif.

gewusst: Rafah is the only border crossing of the Gaza Strip that does not lead into Israel.
In 2024 the Swiss Parliament passed a law banning Hamas in Switzerland.

teile.einleitung: Greta Thunberg is a climate activist from Sweden. At 15 she began going on strike from school to demand more climate protection. This grew into a worldwide youth movement.
wichtigste: Greta Thunberg was born in Stockholm in 2003.
In August 2018 she began her school strike in front of the Swedish parliament.
Her strikes gave rise to the Fridays for Future movement.
In January 2019 she spoke at the World Economic Forum in Davos.
In 2019 she sailed across the Atlantic to the UN climate summit in New York.
The magazine “Time” named her Person of the Year in 2019.

abschnitte.titel: A sign in front of parliament
abschnitte.text: In August 2018 Greta Thunberg, then 15, did not go to school. Instead she sat down with a sign in front of the **Riksdag** in Stockholm, Sweden's parliament. The sign said “School strike for the climate” in Swedish. She wanted politicians to do more against **climate change**. Soon other young people joined in.

Because the strikes took place on Fridays, the movement called itself **Fridays for Future**. Young people all over the world took to the streets. In Switzerland this led to the **Climate Strike**. In many cities tens of thousands of young people demonstrated for more climate protection.

In January 2019 Greta Thunberg spoke to business leaders at the **World Economic Forum** in Davos. She said that people should act as if their own house were on fire. In September 2019 she gave a speech at the **UN climate summit** in New York. With the cry **“How dare you!”** she accused the heads of state of letting young people down.

Greta Thunberg does not fly, because aeroplanes emit a lot of **CO2**. In 2019 she crossed the Atlantic on the racing yacht **“Malizia II”**. The voyage took about two weeks. That same year the US magazine **“Time”** named her Person of the Year. At 16 she was the youngest person ever to receive this honour.

Many people admire Greta Thunberg for her courage and determination. Others criticise the way she presents herself or her demands. She still stands up for other political causes too. What is undisputed is that she has got many young people to take an interest in the **climate**.

gewusst: Greta Thunberg's first strike was completely on her own, with just a home-made sign.
She is still the youngest Person of the Year in the history of “Time” magazine.

teile.einleitung: In November 1985 the US President Ronald Reagan and the Soviet party leader Mikhail Gorbachev met in Geneva. It was their first meeting, in the middle of the Cold War. The summit is seen as the start of an easing of tension between the two superpowers.
wichtigste: The summit lasted from 19 to 21 November 1985.
Reagan represented the USA, Gorbachev the Soviet Union.
The President of the Confederation, Kurt Furgler, received the guests for Switzerland.
Nuclear weapons were at the centre of the talks.
The statement declared that a nuclear war cannot be won and must never be fought.
In 1986 the two met again in Reykjavik.

abschnitte.titel: In the middle of the Cold War
abschnitte.text: The summit took place during the **Cold War**. This is the name for the long period of tension between the **USA** and the **Soviet Union** after the Second World War. Both sides had huge numbers of **nuclear weapons**. **Ronald Reagan** was President of the USA, and **Mikhail Gorbachev** was General Secretary of the Communist Party of the Soviet Union.

Switzerland made Geneva available as a neutral meeting place. The President of the Confederation, **Kurt Furgler**, welcomed Reagan before the summit and stressed Switzerland's role as host. On the first day of talks, the two met at the **Villa Fleur d'Eau**. It is in the municipality of **Versoix**, right on the shore of Lake Geneva.

Reagan and Gorbachev held a one-to-one talk in a pool house in front of a **fire**. That is why the meeting is also called the **Fireside Summit**. The two got to know each other personally. This is seen as important for the trust of the following years.

At the centre was the limiting of **nuclear weapons**. No disarmament treaty was reached in Geneva yet. But in their joint statement, both sides declared that **a nuclear war cannot be won and must never be fought**. This sentence is still often quoted today. The next meeting took place in October 1986 in **Reykjavik** in Iceland.

gewusst: In 1987 Reagan and Gorbachev signed the INF Treaty on intermediate-range missiles in Washington.
On the last day of the Geneva Summit, the two held a joint press conference.

teile.einleitung: The Hague Conventions of 1907 are treaties between many countries. Among other things, they lay down how neutral countries must behave in war. They are still very important for neutral Switzerland today.
wichtigste: The Hague Conventions were adopted in 1907 at the Second Hague Peace Conference.
The Hague is in the Netherlands.
Two conventions govern neutrality: one in war on land, one in war at sea.
A neutral country does not take part in other countries' wars.
Foreign soldiers who flee into a neutral country are disarmed and interned.
A neutral country may defend itself against attacks.

abschnitte.text: **The Hague** is the seat of government of the **Netherlands**. In 1899 and 1907 representatives of many countries met there for the **Hague Peace Conferences**. They wanted to set rules so that wars would be less cruel and disputes could be settled peacefully. In 1907 a total of 13 conventions were adopted. Some of them still apply today.

Two of the conventions govern **neutrality**. One applies to **war on land**, the other to **war at sea**. Aircraft played no part in 1907, which is why there are no separate rules for them. Being neutral means that a country does not take sides in a war between other countries.

A neutral country may not take part in a war. It may not let its own **soldiers** fight for a party to the war. In the other direction, parties to a war may not march **troops** through the territory of a neutral country. This territory is **inviolable**. If a neutral country restricts the export of war material, it must **treat** all parties to the war **equally**.

If soldiers of a party to the war flee onto neutral territory, the neutral country must **disarm** and **intern** them. This means they are housed in a particular place and can no longer take part in the war. Switzerland knew this even earlier: in 1871 it took in the French **Bourbaki Army** and looked after the soldiers.

A neutral country may defend itself if it is attacked. The Hague Convention states that resisting a violation of neutrality is **not a hostile act**. That is why Switzerland has an **army**. It is meant to protect the country and be able to defend its neutrality.

gewusst: In The Hague stands the Peace Palace, where the UN's International Court of Justice sits today.
The Hague Conventions of 1907 are more than a hundred years old and still apply.

teile.einleitung: The HIPC Initiative is a programme that cancels debts for very poor and heavily indebted countries. It was launched in 1996 by the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and the World Bank. The money saved is meant to be used to fight poverty.
wichtigste: HIPC stands for “Heavily Indebted Poor Countries”.
The IMF counts 39 countries that are eligible or possibly eligible.
33 of them are in Africa south of the Sahara.
At the decision point, a country is admitted to the programme.
For full debt relief, a poverty reduction strategy is needed.
From 2005 the MDRI added full cancellation of certain debts to the initiative.

abschnitte.text: Over the decades, many poor countries had taken on large **debts** with other countries and international banks. The interest and repayments ate up a large part of their money. There was hardly anything left for schools, hospitals or roads. That is why the **IMF** and the **World Bank** started the HIPC Initiative in 1996. It is meant to reduce the burden of debt to a bearable level.

The road to debt relief has several stages. At the **decision point**, the IMF and the World Bank decide that a country may take part. After that it already receives some temporary relief. The country must present a **poverty reduction strategy** and carry it out for at least a year. At the **completion point**, it then receives full debt relief.

The IMF counts **39 countries** that are eligible or possibly eligible. 33 of them are in **Africa south of the Sahara**. They are joined by Afghanistan and some countries in Latin America and the Caribbean, for example **Bolivia**, Honduras, Nicaragua, Guyana and Haiti. Bolivia was one of the first countries to complete the process. Almost all the countries have made great progress today.

In 2005 an addition was prepared at the G8 summit: the **Multilateral Debt Relief Initiative**, **MDRI** for short. Countries that have completed the HIPC process receive **full cancellation** of certain debts through it. These are debts to the IMF, the World Bank and the African Development Fund.

Some countries joined only late. **Sudan** reached the decision point in 2021, after the long-time ruler Omar al-Bashir had been overthrown. The war in Sudan from 2023 slowed down the further process. **Eritrea** is the only country that has not yet started the process and has so far received no HIPC relief.

gewusst: Around the year 2000, churches and aid organisations in many countries called for debt relief for poor countries with the “Jubilee” campaign (in German, “Erlassjahr”).
Almost all of the 39 HIPC countries have now completed the whole process.

teile.einleitung: A capital city is the city where a country's government has its seat. Often the parliament works there too. The capital is not always the largest city in a country.
wichtigste: A country's government sits in the capital.
In Switzerland, Bern is officially called the federal city.
The largest Swiss city is Zurich.
Every canton has a capital where the cantonal government sits.
Berlin is the largest capital among Switzerland's neighbouring countries.
Vienna is both a city and an Austrian federal state.

abschnitte.text: In the **capital** there are usually the **government** and the **parliament** of a country. Often there are also embassies of other countries there. The capital is not always the largest city. In Canada, Ottawa is the capital, not Toronto. In Australia it is Canberra, not Sydney. In the USA too, Washington is much smaller than New York.
